content: They play a crucial role in raising awareness, identifying potential users, and referring them to appropriate services. With adequate training and guidance, they can collaborate with service providers in peer counseling, individual follow-ups, collecting user feedback, and conducting impact assessments. Governments, as per the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (CRPD), are obligated to ensure the availability and affordability of high-quality assistive devices and technologies, including prostheses and orthoses. While governments may not directly deliver these services, they are responsible for enacting legislation, formulating policies, preparing national plans, regulating, financing, raising awareness, and promoting prosthetics and orthotics. Governments can foster an environment where services thrive in both public and private sectors by bringing together relevant stakeholders. To achieve this, a national prosthetics and orthotics committee or a similar entity can be established within existing structures for health, rehabilitation, and assistive technology coordination. A national prosthetics and orthotics committee strengthens the coordination of these services. Ideally, this body should be integrated into existing health and rehabilitation frameworks, possibly as a subgroup of a broader entity, provided sufficient attention is given to the specific needs of prosthetics and orthotics. The structure of such a committee depends on the local context. For instance, in India, a prosthetics and orthotics committee within the Rehabilitation Council of India supports education and service delivery in these specialties. A committee with diverse membership and a significant role for the government can coordinate the development of national policies, legislation, and strategic plans while monitoring services to ensure all stakeholders work towards common goals. To be effective, the committee should set clear objectives and meet regularly, adapting to local needs. While many tasks can be delegated through self-governance and professional stewardship, the involvement of relevant government offices at national and local levels may still be necessary. Governments could establish a dedicated office for rehabilitation and assistive technology, coordinated by professional experts, to ensure proper attention to the sector. Civil society organizations are vital in prosthetics and orthotics services as they engage with local populations, raising awareness and increasing treatment uptake among diverse communities. Their advocacy often drives policy development and practice. Service providers, whether public, private (profit or non-profit), non-governmental, or philanthropic, not only deliver direct services but also play a significant role in collecting data for national planning. Health and rehabilitation services are essential for successful prosthetics and orthotics service provision, forming a critical component of the health and rehabilitation continuum. Representatives from these services must be involved in all phases of planning and service development. National and regional training institutions ensure an adequate supply of competent prosthetics and orthotics personnel to meet the country's needs. They are also central to initiating, conducting, and promoting research. Training institutions must be directly involved in workforce and sector planning to address training needs effectively and in a timely manner. In countries without prosthetics or orthotics schools, advice can be sought from institutions in neighboring countries. Professional associations of prosthetists, orthotists, physiotherapists, occupational therapists, nurses, doctors, and other disciplines possess collective knowledge indispensable for planning, developing, and promoting prosthetics and orthotics services. Regional and international associations can provide additional valuable support. Manufacturers and suppliers of components, materials, and consumables should focus on research, development, production, and training to ensure the availability of high-quality, cost-effective materials for prosthetics and orthotics fabrication across various treatment contexts. The international prosthetics and orthotics community plays a significant role in advocacy, international coordination, information exchange, and providing direct technical support and funding for service development. Funding agencies are essential to ensure prosthetics and orthotics services are affordable for all in need, as reliance solely on out-of-pocket payments is unsustainable. Services are typically subsidized by government funds, insurance, charities, corporate social responsibility schemes, and other sources. Governments are responsible for establishing a guiding framework for prosthetics and orthotics services, including national laws, policies, plans, standards, regulations, and rules for licensing service providers and accrediting professionals. This framework should be developed and monitored in collaboration with all national stakeholders. Legislation should align with the CRPD, ensuring recognized rights and revising national laws as necessary. Governments must also enforce these laws. Policies for prosthetics and orthotics services should be formulated in collaboration with stakeholders, ensuring services are affordable, accessible, effective, efficient, safe, and of acceptable quality, adhering to international standards. These policies should be integrated into broader rehabilitation or assistive technology policies, addressing the specific needs of prosthetics and orthotics. A national strategic plan for prosthetics and orthotics services should be part of the national health strategy, linked to development plans, and include detailed goals and steps for establishing, developing, and managing services. This plan should be prepared by all relevant stakeholders and function as a working document, gradually incorporating more information and detailed plans. Governments, in collaboration with stakeholders, should define standards for working methods, processes, practices, infrastructure, and equipment in prosthetics and orthotics services. These standards should facilitate monitoring, auditing, and evaluation of services. International standards, such as those from the International Organization for Standardization (ISO), can serve as models for national standards. Regulation is essential to protect user safety and ensure services are provided professionally by adequately trained personnel using reliable materials and equipment. Governments should regulate prosthetics and orthotics training, professionals, services, products, and the importation and distribution of related components and materials. Mechanisms for implementation, monitoring, and enforcement should be established, including audits and evaluations by multidisciplinary teams of external experts. Licensing ensures that prosthetics and orthotics services are provided only by qualified providers. Governments should establish licensing systems with minimum requirements, including personnel qualifications, adherence to national standards, and accountability. Licensed services must undergo audits and report statistics to the government. Licenses should be renewable periodically. Accreditation ensures that only professionals meeting national competence standards can practice. Governments should organize accreditation mechanisms, including processes for withdrawing accreditation from professionals who commit serious errors or engage in fraudulent activities. Accreditation may be delegated to an independent state regulator. Governments must monitor prosthetics and orthotics services to ensure they align with national policies and plans. Monitoring should include data collection, regular audits, and evaluations of quality and adherence to standards. This process can be conducted directly by the government or delegated to an independent authority. International support is critical in lowand middle-income countries for establishing and improving prosthetics and orthotics services, often in response to disasters. Organizations provide financial and technical support, professional training, policy development, and service delivery tools. Long-term strategies should integrate international support into national systems for sustainable results. International organizations can assist in developing cost-effective service delivery models and building local resources.
